# Study

**Article:** Plasticity Loss in Deep Reinforcement Learning: A Survey

**Authors:** Klein, Luther, McAuliffe, Miklautz, Plant, and Tschiatschek

**DOI/URL:** arXiv:2411.04832v3, 2026

**Replication Type:** Direct

**Computational Environment:** Python 3.12

**Primary Packages:** NumPy 2.4, SciPy 1.17, Matplotlib 3.10, pandas 3.0

**Random Seed:** Not applicable (the mappings are deterministic)

**Repository:** https://github.com/sokpheanal/ANLY735-Replication-Lab-02

# 1. Research Claim

I reproduce Figure 3 of the survey, which visualizes how three categorical target representations turn a value-regression target into a distribution over a fixed support of atoms [@klein2026plasticity].
Two-hot [@schrittwieser2020muzero] places mass on the two atoms bracketing a scalar target; HL-Gauss [@imani2018distributional] integrates a fixed-width Gaussian over each bin; and C51 [@bellemare2017distributional] propagates a full return distribution through the Bellman map and projects it back onto the support.
The "result" being reproduced is the mass each scheme assigns across bins.
There is no accuracy metric here; the object of interest is the shape of the induced distribution.
This figure matters because reformulating regression as classification is one of the survey's mitigation families (Section 5.7) and connects directly to its regression-loss driver (Section 4.4): bounded cross-entropy gradients avoid the parameter-norm growth that error-proportional
MSE gradients produce.

# 2. Replication Strategy

This is a **Proxy** replication of the figure's content.
Figure 3 depicts deterministic mappings defined by published equations rather than an experiment with data, so no original dataset or code is needed to reproduce it: implementing the three formulas exactly regenerates the figure.
What is available is the mathematical definition of each scheme from its source paper and the survey's description.
What I reproduce is the per-bin probability mass each scheme assigns for a chosen target and support.
What must differ is that the original figure is schematic (and, per its caption, redrawn from Farebrother et al. [@farebrother2024stop]), stating no numeric support, target, or Gaussian width; I therefore choose and document those parameters.
The approach is a meaningful check because it forces the definitions to be stated precisely enough to compute, which surfaces exactly
the parameters the schematic leaves implicit.

# 3. Data

There is no dataset.
The inputs are the analyst-chosen quantities that define the mappings.
The support is 5 atoms evenly spaced on the interval [-1, 1], matching the paper's schematic, giving a bin width of 0.5.
Two-hot acts on a scalar target y = -0.20, which falls between the atoms at -0.5 and 0. HL-Gauss is centered on the middle atom (0), matching the paper's symmetric illustration, and uses a Gaussian of standard deviation 0.45, that is 0.9 of a bin width.
C51 acts on a source return distribution Z (a five-point distribution peaked left of center, so the projection visibly shifts mass as in the paper's panel) and propagates it through the Bellman map with reward r = 0.00 and discount gamma = 0.90.
Bin edges for the HL-Gauss integration are the midpoints between adjacent atoms, extended by half a bin at each end. All values are fixed constants in the script; none are learned, sampled, or drawn from external data, so there is no preprocessing and nothing restricted or personal in the repository.

# 4. Method

Each scheme is implemented directly from its defining equation.
**Two-hot**: for a target y between atoms z_lo and z_up, assign mass (z_up - y) / (z_up - z_lo) to z_lo and the complement to z_up, so exactly two atoms are nonzero.
**HL-Gauss**: place N(y, sigma^2) at the target and set each bin's mass to the Gaussian's integral over that bin, computed as a difference of normal CDFs across the bin edges, then renormalize so the mass truncated beyond the support is redistributed.
**C51**: for each source atom z_j with probability p_j, compute the Bellman image Tz_j = clip(r + gamma * z_j, V_min, V_max), locate it between two atoms, and split p_j between them by linear interpolation, accumulating the projected distribution.
Projection indices are clipped to the support to guard against floating-point overshoot at the top atom.
I report, for each scheme, the full per-bin mass vector, the number of nonzero bins, and the entropy of the induced distribution as a compact summary of how concentrated or spread it is. Each distribution is asserted to sum to one.
Software: Python 3.12 with NumPy, SciPy (for the normal CDF), pandas, and Matplotlib.
The figure and the mass table regenerate from `code/reproduce_fig3.ipynb`.

# 5. Results

![Reproduction of Figure 3. Two-hot places all mass on the two atoms bracketing the target y. HL-Gauss integrates a fixed-width Gaussian over the bins. C51 carries the source distribution Z through the Bellman map r + gamma*Z and projects it back onto the support.](figures/fig3_categorical_losses.png)

The three panels reproduce the behavior the figure depicts.
Two-hot assigns 0.40 and 0.60 to the atoms at -0.5 and 0 and zero everywhere else, so only two bins are active and the distribution's entropy is 0.67 nats.
HL-Gauss spreads mass in a bell around the target, with entropy 1.33 nats, acting like label smoothing on the categorical target.
C51 propagates the whole source distribution: the Bellman map shifts it by the reward and contracts it by gamma = 0.90, and the projected distribution (entropy 1.35 nats) is displaced and reshaped relative to the source.
All three distributions integrate to one.
The contrast across panels is the figure's point: the schemes range from maximally sparse (two-hot) to fully distributional (C51), trading simplicity against how much of the target's structure the categorical representation preserves.

# 6. Compare

| Evidence | Original Study | Replication |
|---|---:|---:|
| Two-hot active bins | two neighbors (schematic) | 2 (mass 0.40 / 0.60) |
| HL-Gauss shape | Gaussian over bins (schematic) | bell, entropy 1.33 nats |
| C51 target | full return distribution (schematic) | projected $\Phi(r+\gamma Z)$, entropy 1.35 nats |

Figure 3 is schematic and, per its caption, redrawn from Farebrother et al. [@farebrother2024stop], so it reports no numeric values; the comparison is therefore on mechanism and shape rather than on matching numbers.
On that basis the reproduction is close but not complete: two-hot activates precisely two neighboring atoms, HL-Gauss produces the integrated-Gaussian spread, and C51 yields a projected return distribution.
The one substantive difference is that the original leaves every parameter implicit, whereas the reproduction must fix the support, the target, the Gaussian width, and the C51 reward and discount.
This makes visible a point the schematic hides: the shapes are parameter-dependent.
HL-Gauss's spread is set entirely by sigma, and a narrower sigma would make it approach two-hot, while C51's displacement and width are set by r and gamma.
The figure communicates a family of mechanisms; any single rendering, mine or the original, is one instance of it.

# 7. Reproducibility Check

- [x] Data source documented
- [x] Code runs from beginning to end
- [x] Computational environment identified
- [x] Software/packages documented
- [x] Package versions documented when relevant
- [x] Random seed documented when applicable
- [x] Key preprocessing steps documented
- [x] Evaluation procedure documented
- [x] Repository README provides reproduction instructions

**What was the greatest reproducibility challenge you encountered?**

The figure specifies none of the quantities needed to draw it: the number of atoms, the value range, the scalar target, the HL-Gauss standard deviation, and the C51 reward, discount, and source distribution are all absent.
Because the induced shapes depend on these, reproducing the figure meant recovering each formula from its
source paper and choosing defensible parameters, then documenting them so the result is regenerable.
A minor implementation issue was floating-point overshoot in the C51 projection at the top atom, which required clipping the projection index.

# 8. Extend

The figure shows the representations but not why the survey ties them to plasticity (Section 4.4): regression gradients scale with prediction error and can grow without bound for large-mean targets, driving parameter-norm growth, whereas cross-entropy gradients on a categorical target are bounded regardless of target magnitude.
I would reproduce that claim directly by computing, for a single output unit, the gradient magnitude of the MSE loss and of the cross-entropy loss against a two-hot or HL-Gauss target as the target value is swept across a wide range, and plotting
the two.
The prediction is that the MSE gradient grows linearly with the target while the cross-entropy gradient saturates.
This extends the static figure into a test of the mechanism the survey actually cares about, showing not just what the categorical targets look like but why reformulating regression as classification mitigates the parameter-norm growth associated with plasticity loss.

# Replication Verdict

Select the statement that best represents your findings:

- [ ] **Reproduced** — The central result was substantially reproduced.
- [x] **Partially Reproduced** — Some findings were reproduced, but meaningful differences remain.
- [ ] **Not Reproduced** — The central result was not reproduced.
- [ ] **Not Directly Comparable** — A proxy replication produced useful methodological insight, but numerical comparison is not appropriate.

Each of the three categorical mappings is reproduced exactly at the level of method and behavior: two-hot places mass on the two bracketing atoms by linear interpolation, HL-Gauss integrates a fixed-width Gaussian over the bins, and C51 projects the Bellman image of a return distribution onto the support.
The redrawn figure also matches the paper's two-tier layout, color scheme, and annotations.
It is a partial rather than complete reproduction because Figure 3 is a hand-drawn schematic, redrawn from Farebrother et al., with no underlying data: the illustrative specifics of the C51 panel in particular, namely the exact source distribution and bar heights and the offset-bar-with-horizontal-connector depiction of the Bellman shift, cannot be derived from the definitions and were only approximated.
The verdict is therefore Partially Reproduced.
The methods and their qualitative structure reproduce faithfully, while an exact visual match to an undocumented schematic is not attainable by computation and would amount to tracing rather than replication.
